extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction writers, novelists, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and critical guidance on choosing and applying narrative method (pictorial vs dramatic), point of view, pacing of preparation and climax, and the use of scene and narration in the novel. Emphasizes how subject should dictate method and shows examples (Balzac, Tolstoy) of successes and failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climax's singular task
rubrics_metrics.description: The climax ought to complete, to add the touch that makes the book whole and organic; that is its task, and that only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve the climax to perform just the necessary touch: it should be free to do what it must without any unnecessary distraction. Anything that can be dealt with earlier should be handled before the climax so the climax is not burdened with exposition or extra business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of preparation is no art if it betrays itself at the outset; it is unrecognizable until it attains its end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preparatory material should work stealthily toward the climax. Avoid calling attention to preparation—do not make the reader aware of deliberate foreshadowing or expanded exposition that telegraphs the intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lay up reserve of effect in opening picture
rubrics_metrics.description: Amass in the opening picture the reserve of effect that the book needs; create so much that there is plenty to destroy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build a richly realized initial world (setting, possessions, social position) so that the later ruin or change has visible, accumulative impact. The more fully established the starting scene, the more potent the depiction of its demolition or decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climax suited to form: pictorial vs dramatic
rubrics_metrics.description: Some climaxes are pictorial (an impression of change and decay needing time) rather than a single dramatic incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the story's turning point is a gradual chill or slow decay, treat the climax pictorially: allow time, cumulative detail and gradual diminution rather than forcing a sudden revelation or a single dramatic stroke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repetition to increase intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: When a subject involves a growing catastrophe produced by repeated failures, the book must reiterate one effect with growing intensity—always at the pitch of high hope and sharp disappointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure sequences of similar incidents so that each repetition is heightened by the changing surroundings (e.g., material losses, social decline) and by increased stakes, rather than letting repetition blunt the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method must be dictated by the subject
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose pictorial (omniscient/reflective) or dramatic (strictly scenic) methods based on what the theme requires: inner-growth or panoramic history favors pictorial narration; a subject that 'tells itself' in scenes favors dramatic method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatization through shifting point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a spokesman or shift the point of view so that the author’s assertions are dramatized and gain weight; progress can go from narrator to spokesman to direct enactment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the direct authorial voice weakens the spell, bring in a narrator-character as spokesman or move to scenes enacted in real time so the reader sees events 'while they are passing' instead of receiving a second-hand report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show mind at work rather than rely on retrospective report
rubrics_metrics.description: If the story involves searching exploration of consciousness, it is better to see the mind at work in the agitation that makes the book rather than to have an after-the-fact account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scenes and interior focalization that render thought processes as lived moments; avoid letting important psychological transformation occur only as narrated summary after the fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of strict dramatic form
rubrics_metrics.description: In rigid drama there is no admission of the reader into the private mind of characters; the form is limited to what eye and ear can witness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not force a strictly scenic/dramatic form where the subject demands inner access, panoramic survey, or the study of a temperament; strict drama grants compactness and objectivity but sacrifices internal perspective and breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial (reflective) narration for large or panoramic subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictorial books call for a narrator who contemplates facts and creates an impression; they allow generalization and panoramic survey that strict scenic method cannot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For stories that are large in scope, span time, or require synthesis and reflection, employ an authorial or chosen narrator to gather experience, summarize, and compose a vision rather than attempting to enact everything scene by scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use dramatic method inside pictorial works
rubrics_metrics.description: A pictorial book may use the dramatic method by entrusting effect to momentary reactions and letting the shapes of thought tell their own story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in an overall reflective work, allow scenes and moment-to-moment consciousness to 'perform' parts of the story so the narrator's voice can recede and the reader gains directness and immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and condensation of initial material
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the opening situation must present a great deal (e.g., all of Anna's past and present) the space must be tightly packed; the method should most condense and concentrate representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the plot forces a character into a critical action early, compress and intensify the initial presentation so the reader fully comprehends the character's background and stakes; avoid leaving crucial past-life context thin or implicit before a major crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-reliance on a habitual method
rubrics_metrics.description: An author should not blindly use the method congenial to him irrespective of what the story requires; misfit of method to subject can damage effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether your favored habit (e.g., scenic immediacy or panoramic reflection) actually serves the material; be willing to alter technique to fit the demands of particular stories to avoid miscalculations like abruptness or inadequate preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small scenes as enrichment, not diversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Passing half-pages or small scenes can make a character's life fuller and speed the story by augmenting tone and the value of lives watched.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid, concentrated glimpses of incident to enrich characters' interiority and to accumulate tone; such small scenes should contribute to a character's completeness and readiness for climax rather than being mere digressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let repetition dilute force—use setting's alteration to renew it
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of similar incidents can be renewed and increased in force by showing the spreading devastation around the central figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a narrative requires repeated setbacks, make each repetition carry new visual or social consequences (loss of treasures, family impoverishment, shrinking reputation) so the repetition registers as intensification not monotony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point-of-view consistency vs necessary shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing who 'tells' the story and how often to shift determines whether the work is dramatic, pictorial, or mixed; dramatic purity implies the reader's single point of view, pictorial works require an outside beholder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide early whether to keep the reader always at the eye-of-the-scene (dramatic) or to adopt an outside, knowing perspective (pictorial); mixing is possible but must be managed so that shifts are motivated by subject and do not produce confusion or dilute authority.
